title: Procurement and Vendor Management for Architects
objectives: Influence procurement to get better technology outcomes
Navigate the Procurement Act 2023 and government commercial frameworks
Write technical requirements that attract good suppliers without constraining innovation
Assess vendor proposals and identify risks that suppliers omit
Manage vendor relationships and prevent lock-in through architecture
whyThisMatters:
Most government technology is delivered partly or entirely by suppliers. Whether you are procuring a platform, a development team, a managed service, or a specialist product, the procurement process determines what you can build, how much it costs, and how much control you retain. Yet architects are frequently excluded from procurement decisions, or included too late to influence them meaningfully.

The Procurement Act 2023, which came into force on 24 February 2025, represents the most significant reform of UK public procurement in decades. It replaces the EU-derived procurement rules with a regime designed to be simpler, more transparent, and more commercially flexible. Alongside this, the Sourcing Playbook (refreshed 2025) and the new Contract Management Playbook (March 2026) set expectations for how departments manage their commercial relationships.

As an architect, you may not run procurements — that is the commercial team's role — but you shape them. You define what needs to be procured (the technical requirements), you evaluate what suppliers offer (the technical assessment), you manage the relationship during delivery (the architectural oversight), and you plan for exit (the architectural independence). Getting these wrong locks your department into expensive, inflexible arrangements for years.

content.heading: The Procurement Act 2023 and What It Means for Architects
content.body:
The Procurement Act 2023, which came into force on 24 February 2025, replaced the EU-derived Public Contracts Regulations 2015 with a UK-specific regime. While procurement is fundamentally a commercial activity, architects need to understand the new framework because it shapes what you can buy, how quickly you can buy it, and how much flexibility you have.

Key changes relevant to architects:

The new competitive flexible procedure gives contracting authorities more freedom in how they structure procurements. Instead of being constrained to the open procedure, restricted procedure, or competitive dialogue, authorities can design bespoke procedures that suit their needs. For technology procurements, this means you can structure evaluations that genuinely test technical capability — demonstrations, proof-of-concept exercises, or iterative dialogue — rather than relying solely on written proposals.

The Central Digital Platform (an expanded Find a Tender Service) provides a single place where all procurement opportunities are published and where suppliers register their details. For architects assessing the market, this provides better visibility of what has been procured previously and what suppliers are available.

Transparency requirements are significantly expanded. The entire contract lifecycle — from planning through market engagement, tendering, and implementation — is now tracked and published. For architects, this means your technical requirements and evaluation criteria will be more visible, and your vendor assessments need to be more rigorously documented.

The existing government commercial frameworks remain available alongside the new Act. G-Cloud provides access to cloud hosting, cloud software, and cloud support services. Digital Outcomes and Specialists 7 (DOS7) provides access to digital, data, and technology services delivered in line with the Service Standard. Crown Commercial Service frameworks cover hardware, telecoms, and specialist technology. These frameworks offer faster procurement routes than open competition — typically weeks rather than months.

The Sourcing Playbook (the current iteration of what was originally the Outsourcing Playbook) sets expectations for how departments approach service delivery decisions — including whether to build in-house, outsource, or use a mixed model. The architect's input into this make-or-buy decision is critical.

content.heading: Writing Technical Requirements That Work
content.body:
Technical requirements in a procurement specification determine what suppliers offer. Write them too tightly and you constrain innovation — suppliers can only offer exactly what you described. Write them too loosely and you get proposals that do not meet your needs. The skill is finding the productive middle.

Specify outcomes, not implementations. 'The system must process 10,000 applications per day with 99.9% availability and sub-3-second response times' is an outcome specification. 'The system must use Kubernetes on AWS with PostgreSQL' is an implementation specification. Outcome specifications attract more diverse and potentially better solutions because suppliers can offer their best approach rather than implementing your pre-determined design.

Be specific about constraints that genuinely constrain. If data must be hosted in the UK for legal reasons, state that as a hard constraint. If you must integrate with a specific existing system, specify the interface. If you must use GOV.UK One Login for citizen authentication, state that. But distinguish between genuine constraints and preferences — a constraint eliminates options; a preference informs scoring.

Define evaluation criteria that test architectural quality. Evaluation criteria determine what suppliers optimise for. If you only evaluate on cost and delivery timeline, you get cheap, fast solutions that may be unmaintainable. Include criteria for: architectural quality (separation of concerns, modularity, standards compliance), maintainability (documentation, test coverage, deployment approach), security (threat modelling, secure development practices), accessibility (WCAG compliance approach), and exit (data portability, IP ownership, technology transferability).

Avoid specifying brand names unless genuinely necessary. 'Must integrate with our Oracle database' is acceptable if you have an Oracle database. 'Must use Oracle' when you are choosing a new database is an unjustified constraint that may exclude better options. The Technology Code of Practice prefers open standards and open source — your requirements should reflect this.

Include non-functional requirements explicitly. Suppliers optimise for what is evaluated. If performance, scalability, security, and accessibility are not in the requirements, suppliers will not invest in them. Define your NFRs clearly and make them evaluation criteria.

content.heading: Evaluating Vendor Proposals: The Architect's Eye
content.body:
When evaluating supplier proposals, architects bring a perspective that commercial evaluators cannot — the ability to assess whether a proposed solution will actually work, scale, and remain maintainable over time.

Look for what is missing. Suppliers optimise their proposals to look attractive. They emphasise strengths and minimise weaknesses. Your job is to identify what is not mentioned. If a proposal describes a complex integration but does not mention error handling, that is a risk. If it promises high availability but does not describe the failover mechanism, that is a gap. If it proposes a microservices architecture but does not address operational complexity, the supplier may not have thought it through.

Challenge scalability claims. 'The system is highly scalable' is meaningless without specifics. Ask: scalable to what level? Through what mechanism? At what cost? Has this been demonstrated at the claimed scale? A supplier claiming their system handles millions of transactions should be able to describe the architecture that enables this and provide evidence from comparable deployments.

Assess the technology stack critically. Is the proposed technology mature and well-supported? Does it have a clear roadmap? Is there a community and marketplace for skills? Is it aligned with government standards (open source, cloud-first, open standards)? A proposal built on niche or proprietary technology creates dependency and recruitment risk.

Evaluate the exit strategy. Can you leave this supplier without losing your data, your configuration, or your operational capability? Proposals that store data in proprietary formats, require proprietary tooling to operate, or do not address intellectual property transfer are creating lock-in. The Sourcing Playbook explicitly requires departments to plan for exit from the start.

Test for honesty. The best suppliers are honest about limitations. A proposal that claims to do everything perfectly is less credible than one that acknowledges trade-offs and explains how they will be managed. Look for: acknowledgement of risks and mitigation strategies, honest assessment of what the product does not do, and clear statements about what additional investment would be needed.

Request demonstrations for critical capabilities. Written proposals can describe anything. A working demonstration reveals reality. For technology procurements, consider including a demonstration or proof-of-concept stage where shortlisted suppliers show their solution working rather than just describing it. The competitive flexible procedure under the Procurement Act 2023 explicitly enables this.

content.heading: Preventing Vendor Lock-In Through Architecture
content.body:
Vendor lock-in occurs when switching from one supplier to another becomes so expensive or risky that you are effectively trapped regardless of the supplier's performance or pricing. Lock-in is government's most common procurement failure mode — and it is primarily an architecture problem.

Lock-in mechanisms include: proprietary data formats (you cannot extract your data in a usable form), proprietary interfaces (your integrations only work with this specific product), intellectual property restrictions (the supplier owns the code and designs), knowledge dependency (only this supplier understands the system), and contractual restrictions (exit is prohibitively expensive or complex).

Architecture decisions that prevent lock-in:

Open standards at every boundary. If your data is stored in open formats and your integrations use open standard APIs, switching to a different product that also supports those standards becomes feasible. This is why the Technology Code of Practice emphasises open standards.

Separation of data from application. Your data should be extractable from any application that processes it. Architecture that stores data in application-specific formats or structures creates data lock-in even if the application itself is replaceable.

Modular architecture with well-defined interfaces. If your system is composed of independent modules that communicate through APIs, you can replace one module (and its supplier) without replacing the whole system. A monolithic solution from a single supplier creates whole-system lock-in.

Intellectual property clarity. Ensure your contract specifies that you own the architecture designs, data models, and any bespoke code developed for you. The Sourcing Playbook requires this, but it must be reflected in your technical specifications.

Knowledge transfer as a deliverable. Require suppliers to transfer knowledge (documentation, training, operational handover) as a contractual obligation throughout delivery, not just at the end. If knowledge exists only in the supplier's team, you are locked in regardless of what the contract says.

Multi-vendor architecture. Where feasible, use different suppliers for different components of your system. This prevents any single supplier from having total control and creates competitive tension. But balance this against integration complexity — too many suppliers creates coordination overhead.

content.heading: Managing Vendors During Delivery
content.body:
Procurement ends when the contract is signed. The architecture relationship with the vendor continues throughout delivery and into operations. Poor vendor management during delivery is how good procurements produce bad outcomes.

Architectural oversight means ensuring the supplier delivers what was proposed and agreed, not a degraded version optimised for their profitability. Common vendor behaviours to watch for: substituting less experienced staff than proposed, reducing the scope of non-functional testing, deferring documentation to the end (where it never gets done), taking shortcuts in security implementation, and accumulating technical debt that will become your problem after the contract ends.

Architecture governance should include the vendor's work. Their design decisions should go through your Design Authority or architecture review process. Their ADRs should be part of your ADR repository. Their code should meet your quality standards. This is not micromanagement — it is ensuring architectural coherence between in-house and supplier-delivered components.

The Contract Management Playbook (published March 2026) provides comprehensive guidance on managing contracts throughout their lifecycle. Key principles include: maintaining oversight proportionate to risk and value, regular performance review against defined service levels, proactive identification of delivery risks, and planning for contract end (extension, re-procurement, or transition) well in advance.

As architect, your specific responsibilities during vendor-delivered work include: reviewing architecture decisions and designs for quality and alignment, verifying non-functional requirements are being met (not just functional delivery), ensuring documentation and knowledge transfer are happening continuously, monitoring technical debt accumulation in vendor-delivered code, and planning the transition at contract end — whether that is to a new vendor, to in-house operation, or to a different solution entirely.

content.heading: The Make-or-Buy Decision
content.body:
The most fundamental procurement decision is whether to build something yourself, buy something off the shelf, or commission someone else to build it. This decision has profound architecture implications.

Build in-house when: the capability is core to your mission and you need full control, the requirement is unique to government and no commercial product fits, you have (or can recruit) the skills to build and maintain it, or the Technology Code of Practice principle of open source supports a bespoke, open solution. Government has built excellent services in-house: GOV.UK itself, GOV.UK Notify, GOV.UK Pay. These are services where government needed full control and the problem was unique enough that no commercial product was suitable.

Buy off-the-shelf when: the requirement is generic (email, document management, project management, CRM), commercial products are mature and well-supported, the cost of customisation is less than the cost of building, and you can accept the product's constraints. But be honest about the customisation cost — a product that requires 60% customisation is not off-the-shelf; it is a platform for bespoke development at a premium.

Commission a supplier when: you need the capability but lack the skills or capacity in-house, the requirement is specific to your organisation but does not need to be built by your organisation, or you need to move faster than in-house recruitment and team-building allows. Most government digital services use a mixed model: in-house architects and product people defining the service, with supplier development teams building it under architectural oversight.

The Sourcing Playbook requires departments to consider all delivery options — not just outsourcing by default. For architects, this means you need to assess your organisation's capability honestly. Can your team build this to the quality required? Can they maintain it long term? Do they have the specialist skills (security, performance engineering, data science) that the service requires? If not, what is the most effective way to access those skills — hire permanently, contract short-term, or outsource a component?

The architecture should be designed to support whichever delivery model you choose — and to allow the delivery model to change over time. A system architected so that only one specific supplier can maintain it is locked in regardless of what the contract says about exit. A system architected with clear interfaces, documented decisions, and standard technologies can transition between delivery models as circumstances change.

workedExample.title: Procuring a Case Management Platform for DESNZ
workedExample.context: DESNZ needs a case management platform to support 200 caseworkers processing energy compliance cases. The current system is a spreadsheet-based manual process that cannot scale. The programme board has decided to procure rather than build, based on the assessment that case management is a generic capability and commercial products are mature. The Solution Architect must define the technical requirements, support the procurement, and evaluate supplier proposals.
workedExample.approach:
The architect works with the commercial team through the procurement lifecycle.

Phase 1 — Requirements Definition (3 weeks):
The architect runs workshops with caseworkers and operational managers to understand the workflows, data requirements, and pain points. They produce an outcome-based specification rather than a feature list. Key requirements include: configurable workflow engine (policy changes 4-6 times per year), integration with GOV.UK Notify for citizen communications, integration with the departmental data warehouse for reporting, role-based access control aligned with existing Active Directory groups, audit trail for all case actions (legal requirement), and accessible interface meeting WCAG 2.2 AA.

Critically, the architect also defines anti-lock-in requirements: data must be exportable in open formats (CSV, JSON), the API must follow GDS API standards (REST, JSON, OpenAPI documented), and all configuration and workflow definitions must be exportable for migration. These requirements are non-negotiable hard constraints.

Phase 2 — Market Assessment (2 weeks):
Using the Digital Marketplace (G-Cloud for SaaS products, DOS7 for implementation support), the architect identifies 8 potential products. They review published documentation and arrange brief demonstrations with the top 5 to assess fit against requirements.

Phase 3 — Procurement (6 weeks via G-Cloud framework):
The commercial team runs the procurement through G-Cloud, which allows direct award to a single supplier if only one product meets requirements, or further competition if multiple do. The architect provides weighted evaluation criteria: functional fit (30%), technical quality including accessibility and standards compliance (25%), integration capability (20%), data portability and exit (15%), cost (10%). Note: cost is only 10% — the architect has argued successfully that the cheapest product is not necessarily the best value if it creates lock-in or cannot be integrated.

Phase 4 — Evaluation (3 weeks):
Three shortlisted suppliers provide detailed proposals and demonstrations. The architect's evaluation focuses on: how configurable are the workflows without code changes? How does the product integrate with external systems — standard APIs or proprietary connectors? Can the department extract all data in open formats if they need to move to a different product? How does the product handle accessibility — is it WCAG 2.2 AA compliant by default or does it require configuration? What is the vendor's technology roadmap — will the product remain current and supported?
workedExample.outcome: The evaluation selects a platform that scores highest on integration capability and data portability, despite being marginally more expensive than the cheapest option. The architect justifies this to the programme board: 'The £40,000 annual cost difference is insurance against lock-in. If we need to switch platforms in three years, the data portability of this product means migration costs approximately £200,000 rather than £800,000 for the cheaper alternative that stores data in proprietary formats.' The board approves. The platform is implemented in 4 months with the architect providing architectural oversight of the configuration and integration work.
workedExample.lessonsLearned: Including data portability and anti-lock-in requirements as hard constraints from the start was essential — it eliminated three products that would have scored well on features but created long-term dependency. Weighting cost at only 10% was initially challenged by the finance team but proved correct — the selected product's integration capabilities saved an estimated £150,000 in bespoke integration work compared to the cheapest alternative that had poor API support. The outcome-based specification attracted more innovative proposals than a feature-list specification would have.

civilServiceScenario.title: The Vendor That Holds All the Cards
civilServiceScenario.background: A department has operated a critical citizen-facing service on a proprietary platform for 7 years under a contract with a single supplier. The contract expires in 12 months. The supplier has indicated that renewal pricing will increase by 40% — from £2.8 million to £3.9 million per year. The department's only alternatives are: accept the price increase, migrate to a different platform (estimated £4 million and 18 months), or bring the service in-house (estimated £3 million and 12 months but requires hiring 8 developers the department does not currently have). The supplier knows the department's weak position — the data is in proprietary formats, the integrations use proprietary APIs, and only the supplier's team understands the system's configuration.
civilServiceScenario.challenge: You must advise the programme board on the best path forward given the time, cost, and risk constraints. You must also propose architecture principles for future procurements that prevent this situation recurring.
constraints: The service processes 2 million transactions per year and cannot be interrupted
Data is stored in a proprietary format with no documented export capability
Integrations use vendor-specific APIs, not open standards
No departmental staff understand the system configuration — all knowledge is with the vendor
The department has no spare development capacity for a migration
Budget for 2026-27 is already committed — additional funding requires a business case to the investment committee
The minister is aware of the situation and considers it unacceptable that a supplier can hold the department to ransom
Similar situations exist with two other vendors in the department
The Sourcing Playbook requires exit planning from contract start — this was not done 7 years ago
civilServiceScenario.yourRole: You are the Solution Architect advising the programme board and proposing long-term architecture principles to prevent recurrence.
civilServiceScenario.discussion:
This is a common scenario in government — the consequence of procurements that prioritised short-term cost over long-term flexibility. The architect's short-term advice must be pragmatic: in 12 months, a full migration is probably not achievable for a critical service. The realistic options are: negotiate the renewal (from a weak position, but the supplier also risks losing the contract entirely if the department commits to migration), or negotiate a shorter extension (2 years instead of 5) while running a parallel procurement for the replacement.

The long-term architecture principles to prevent recurrence include: mandatory data portability requirements in all technology contracts, open standard APIs for all integrations, continuous knowledge transfer as a contractual obligation, regular export testing (can we actually extract our data?), and architecture reviews that specifically assess lock-in risk. These principles should be embedded in the department's architecture governance and reflected in commercial templates.

The minister's frustration is a political opportunity — use it to secure investment in the architecture principles and practices that prevent lock-in, not just to fix this one instance.

practiceArtefact.description: Write the technical requirements section for a procurement of a cloud-based document management service for DESNZ. The service will store 5 million documents (compliance reports, applications, certificates), be used by 500 internal staff, and must integrate with the existing case management system and GOV.UK Notify. Produce requirements that are outcome-based, include anti-lock-in provisions, and align with government standards.
practiceArtefact.guidance: Structure requirements as: Functional Requirements (what the system must do), Non-Functional Requirements (how well it must do it), Integration Requirements (what it must connect to), Standards Requirements (what standards it must comply with), and Exit Requirements (what must be possible when the contract ends). Use outcome language ('must enable') rather than implementation language ('must use'). Include evaluation criteria weights.
practiceArtefact.modelAnswer:
**Technical Requirements: Cloud Document Management Service**

**1. Functional Requirements:**
FR1: Must store, version, and retrieve documents up to 100MB in size
FR2: Must support at least 5 million documents with capacity for 20% annual growth
FR3: Must provide full-text search across all document content and metadata within 3 seconds
FR4: Must support configurable retention policies with automated enforcement (deletion after defined period)
FR5: Must provide role-based access control with at least 10 configurable permission levels
FR6: Must support document workflows (review, approve, publish) with configurable routing
FR7: Must provide audit trail of all document actions (view, edit, delete, share) with timestamp and user identity
FR8: Must support bulk import from existing file shares and legacy document stores

**2. Non-Functional Requirements:**
NFR1: Availability 99.9% during business hours (08:00-18:00 Mon-Fri), 99.5% at other times
NFR2: Response time for document retrieval under 2 seconds for documents up to 50MB
NFR3: Must be accessible, meeting WCAG 2.2 Level AA for all user-facing interfaces
NFR4: Data must be hosted in the UK (data sovereignty requirement)
NFR5: Must support 500 concurrent users without performance degradation
NFR6: Must meet Cyber Essentials Plus certification as a minimum security standard
NFR7: Must support multi-factor authentication for all users

**3. Integration Requirements:**
IR1: Must provide a REST API following GDS API technical and data standards (JSON, OpenAPI 3.0 documented)
IR2: Must integrate with DESNZ Active Directory for user authentication (SAML 2.0 or OIDC)
IR3: Must support webhook-based event notifications for document state changes
IR4: Must enable integration with GOV.UK Notify for document-related user notifications via API
IR5: Must provide a documented API for the case management system to link documents to cases

**4. Standards Requirements:**
SR1: Must use open standards for data storage and exchange (not proprietary formats)
SR2: Must comply with the Technology Code of Practice
SR3: Must follow Secure by Design principles
SR4: Must support the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard if any algorithmic processing is used

**5. Exit Requirements:**
ER1: All documents must be exportable in their original format with complete metadata in CSV/JSON
ER2: All configuration (workflows, permissions, retention policies) must be exportable in a documented format
ER3: Complete data export must be achievable within 30 days of request
ER4: Supplier must provide 6 months of transition support during any exit
ER5: No proprietary data formats that prevent migration to alternative platforms

**Evaluation Criteria:**
| Criterion | Weight |
|---|---|
| Functional fit | 25% |
| Non-functional compliance (including accessibility) | 20% |
| Integration capability (API quality, standards compliance) | 20% |
| Security and data protection | 15% |
| Exit and portability | 10% |
| Cost (whole life over 5 years) | 10% |

reflectiveQuestions: Think about a vendor relationship in your department. Does the architecture give you genuine choice about whether to continue with that vendor, or are you effectively locked in? What would it cost to switch?
When did you last include data portability and exit requirements in a procurement specification? If never, what would happen if your current vendor doubled their prices?
How involved are architects in procurement evaluation in your organisation? Are you evaluating proposals, or does the commercial team handle everything?
Have you ever recommended against a particular technology because of lock-in risk, even though it was technically attractive? How was that recommendation received?
How would you assess whether a vendor's proposal is genuinely achievable versus aspirational marketing? What signals distinguish the two?

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the most significant change the Procurement Act 2023 introduces for technology procurements?
options: All technology must now be procured through a single framework
The competitive flexible procedure allows authorities to design bespoke evaluation processes
Suppliers must now be UK-based companies
All procurements must use the lowest-cost approach
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The competitive flexible procedure gives contracting authorities more freedom in structuring procurements. For technology, this enables demonstrations, proof-of-concept stages, and iterative dialogue rather than relying solely on written proposals — leading to better-informed procurement decisions.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the primary purpose of including exit requirements in a technology procurement?
options: To reduce the initial contract price
To ensure the department can leave the vendor without losing data or capability (preventing lock-in)
To penalise the vendor for poor performance
To satisfy audit requirements without practical application
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Exit requirements prevent vendor lock-in by ensuring the department can extract its data, transfer its configuration, and transition to an alternative without prohibitive cost or risk. The Sourcing Playbook requires exit planning from contract start.

knowledgeCheck.question: When writing technical requirements for a procurement, what approach produces the best outcomes?
options: Specify the exact technology stack the supplier must use
Specify outcomes and constraints rather than implementation details
Copy requirements from a previous similar procurement
Let the supplier define the requirements based on their product capabilities
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Outcome-based specifications ('must process 10,000 applications per day with 99.9% availability') attract more diverse and innovative proposals than implementation specifications ('must use Kubernetes on AWS'). They allow suppliers to offer their best approach while ensuring the department's needs are met.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which government framework allows fastest procurement of cloud services?
options: Open competition under the Procurement Act 2023
G-Cloud framework through the Digital Marketplace
DOS7 (Digital Outcomes and Specialists 7)
Crown Commercial Service Technology Products framework
knowledgeCheck.explanation: G-Cloud allows direct award to a single supplier or further competition among shortlisted suppliers, typically completing in weeks rather than months. It provides access to cloud hosting, cloud software, and cloud support services through pre-approved suppliers.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the most effective architecture decision for preventing vendor lock-in?
options: Using the same vendor for all components to ensure compatibility
Requiring open standards at every integration boundary and open formats for all data
Choosing the largest vendor because they are least likely to fail
Signing the longest possible contract to lock in current pricing
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Open standards at integration boundaries and open formats for data storage ensure that any component can be replaced with an alternative that supports the same standards. This maintains genuine choice throughout the contract lifecycle, regardless of vendor behaviour.
